diagram_name: Where the Minutes Go in a Traditional School Day
chapter_title: The Building Blocks of Schools, Students, and Learning
learning_objective: The learner will differentiate the minutes of an illustrative middle-school day into whole-class direct instruction, practice, and non-instructional time, estimating the direct-instruction total to within 10 minutes.
specification:
Type: chart **sim-id:** school-day-minute-map
**Library:** Chart.js
**Status:** Specified
**Bloom Level:** Analyze
**Bloom Verb:** differentiate
**Learning Objective:** The learner will differentiate the minutes of an illustrative middle-school day into whole-class direct instruction, practice, and non-instructional time, estimating the direct-instruction total to within 10 minutes. **Template:** https://github.com/dmccreary/ai-strategy-for-education/tree/main/docs/sims/school-day-comparison-timeline
**Prerequisites:** school day, direct instruction, the I-do/we-do/you-do pattern, classroom (all defined in the section "The School Day and Direct Instruction" above). **Evidence of Mastery:** Before the chart is revealed, the learner enters two estimates: (a) total minutes of whole-class direct instruction in the day, and (b) which category is the largest single use of time. Estimate (a) is correct when it is within ±10 minutes of 100. Estimate (b) is correct when it is "Whole-class direct instruction" or "Practice" (they tie at 100 minutes each). Viewing the chart after reveal is exploration. **Misconceptions:** (1) Most of the school day is spent with a teacher explaining new material. (2) Almost all of a seven-hour day is academic time. (3) Non-instructional time (passing, lunch, settling in) is negligible. **Instructional Rationale:** Analyze-level differentiation requires the learner to separate a familiar whole (a school day) into categories and see their proportions. Committing to an estimate before the reveal exposes the learner's mental model so the chart can correct it. **Content:** The illustrative schedule, shown as a list before the reveal: | Time | Block | Minutes | |---|---|---| | 8:00–8:10 | Homeroom | 10 | | 8:10–8:15 | Passing | 5 | | 8:15–9:05 | Period 1: English | 50 | | 9:05–9:10 | Passing | 5 | | 9:10–10:00 | Period 2: Mathematics | 50 | | 10:00–10:05 | Passing | 5 | | 10:05–10:55 | Period 3: Science | 50 | | 10:55–11:00 | Passing | 5 | | 11:00–11:50 | Period 4: Social Studies | 50 | | 11:50–12:20 | Lunch | 30 | | 12:20–12:25 | Passing | 5 | | 12:25–1:15 | Period 5: World Language | 50 | | 1:15–1:20 | Passing | 5 | | 1:20–2:10 | Period 6: Art | 50 | | 2:10–2:15 | Passing | 5 | | 2:15–3:05 | Period 7: Physical Education | 50 | Each of the five academic periods (Periods 1–5) is divided as: 5 minutes settling and attendance, 20 minutes whole-class direct instruction, 20 minutes guided and independent practice, 5 minutes wrap-up. Category totals revealed in the chart: | Category | Minutes | Share of 425 minutes | |---|---|---| | Whole-class direct instruction | 100 | 23.5% | | Guided and independent practice | 100 | 23.5% | | Arts and physical education | 100 | 23.5% | | Settling, attendance, and wrap-up | 50 | 11.8% | | Passing time | 35 | 8.2% | | Lunch | 30 | 7.1% | | Homeroom | 10 | 2.4% | | Total | 425 | 100% | **Provenance:** Illustrative composite schedule written for this chapter; the sim must label it "Illustrative schedule." Period lengths follow the chapter's statement that middle-school periods run 45 to 55 minutes. **Rules:** Shares are minutes ÷ 425, shown to one decimal place. Estimate (a) is correct when |estimate − 100| <= 10. Estimate (a) accepts whole numbers from 0 to 425. Estimate (b) is chosen from the seven category names; either of the two tied categories named in Evidence of Mastery is correct. **Learner Activity:** 1. The learner reads the schedule and enters estimate (a) and selects estimate (b). 2. The learner reveals the chart. The day appears as categories with minutes and shares, and the learner's estimates appear beside the true values. 3. The learner selects any category to see which blocks of the schedule contribute to it. 4. The learner should notice that whole-class direct instruction is less than a quarter of the day, and that non-instructional categories (settling, passing, lunch, homeroom) add up to 125 minutes, more than direct instruction. **Feedback:** One attempt per estimate before reveal. Estimate (a) correct: "Within 10 minutes — 100 minutes of the 425-minute day is whole-class direct instruction." Incorrect, too high: "Higher than the schedule shows. Teachers explain new material for about 20 minutes of each 50-minute academic period, and only five of the seven periods are academic." Incorrect, too low: "Lower than the schedule shows — five academic periods with about 20 minutes of explanation each make 100 minutes." Estimate (b) correct: "Right — direct instruction and practice tie at 100 minutes, and arts and PE also take 100." Incorrect: "That category is smaller. Three categories tie at 100 minutes each." After reveal, the estimates cannot be changed; a "Try again" action clears them and hides the chart. **Starting State:** The schedule list is visible, the chart is hidden, and the prompt reads "In this seven-hour day, how many minutes does a student spend listening to a teacher explain new material to the whole class?" **Chapter Anchors:** The chapter states that a typical U.S. school day runs about six and a half to seven hours and that middle-school periods run 45 to 55 minutes. The worked example lesson uses a 50-minute period. The illustrative day totals 425 minutes, with 100 minutes of whole-class direct instruction.
